strengths: The paper addresses a consequential bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction with a practical, training-free modification. Preserving the pretrained backbone and task heads makes the approach potentially useful for existing VGGT and π3 deployments.

Table 1 demonstrates meaningful speedups with small accuracy losses at conservative settings. For 200-frame VGGT, S25 reduces runtime from 18 to 8.5 seconds while RRA@5 changes from 83.9 to 83.1 and RTA@5 from 79.9 to 79.6. For full-length π3, runtime falls from 27.9 to 13.6 seconds with approximately one percentage point of rotation-recall loss.

Evaluation spans two backbones, multiple pose and reconstruction benchmarks, and different sequence lengths. The supplementary parameter sweeps provide substantially more evidence than isolated operating points.

The special-token treatment has useful empirical support: Figure A-1 shows improved reconstruction robustness at high sparsity, particularly on ETH3D and NRGBD. Figure A-2 also supports the decision to avoid training additional projections.
weaknesses: The headline claim of up to 4× acceleration with comparable performance conflates different operating regimes. In Table 1, 100-frame VGGT-S75 achieves approximately 3.8× acceleration, but RRA@5 falls from 84.8 to 58.1 and RTA@5 from 81.3 to 61.5. Full-length π3-S75 similarly reduces RRA@5 from 75.8 to 50.0. Stable ATE does not negate these substantial relative-pose losses. The evidence supports a useful accuracy–speed trade-off, rather than broadly preserved quality at the largest speedups.

The contribution beyond existing sparse-attention methods is insufficiently isolated. Pooled query–key scoring and block-sparse execution closely follow the cited literature; preserving special-token interactions is the clearest demonstrated adaptation. There is no direct accuracy–runtime comparison against unmodified SpargeAttention, and no ablation separating CDF-only, top-k-only, and combined selection. Consequently, the necessity and benefit of the proposed selection rule remain uncertain.

Runtime attribution is incomplete for an efficiency-focused paper. Figure 1 identifies FlashAttention2, but Table 1 does not fully specify matched dense/sparse kernel configurations, numerical precision, timing methodology, or mask-generation and token-reordering overhead. The 100-frame S25 result gives a 2.7× speedup despite its relatively conservative sparsification, indicating that skipped attention entries alone do not explain the gain. A dense run through the same execution backend would help distinguish algorithmic savings from implementation differences.

The attention analysis is suggestive rather than conclusive. Visual correspondences and average/maximum attention statistics do not quantify how much true attention mass the pooled block predictor retains. Dropping middle layers establishes sensitivity to removing those layers, but does not establish that they primarily perform correspondence search or explain the effectiveness of the proposed mask. The geometric interpretation should therefore remain a hypothesis.

Several specification issues hinder reproducibility. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask before softmax, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero probability; exclusion requires negative-infinity masking or an equivalent restricted softmax. Section 4.2 does not explain how patch and special-token interactions share the correct softmax normalization. Section 5 also defines sparsity as the fraction computed while using formulas for the fraction skipped, and Table 1 does not clearly map S25/S50/S75 to the reported threshold settings and realized sparsity. These are partly correctable exposition issues, but they concern the core operator and operating points.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction. Its training-free retrofit preserves existing backbones and applies to both VGGT and π3, making the approach potentially useful.

Table 1 demonstrates worthwhile operating points with modest accuracy loss: on 200-frame Tanks & Temples inputs, VGGT-S25 reduces runtime from 18 to 8.5 seconds while RRA@5 changes from 83.9 to 83.1. Such efficiency gains are valuable without improving benchmark accuracy.

Evaluation spans nine datasets, two architectures, and multiple sequence lengths. The supplementary special-token ablation supports retaining dense interactions involving camera/register tokens, particularly for reconstruction at high sparsity. The learned-projection ablation also provides useful evidence favoring the simpler training-free approach.
weaknesses: The headline claim of approximately 4× faster inference with comparable performance overstates the demonstrated joint trade-off. In Table 1, the 100-frame VGGT configuration approaching 4× acceleration reduces RRA@5 from 84.8 to 58.1 and RTA@5 from 81.3 to 61.5. At full sequence length, π3-S75 reduces RRA@5 from 75.8 to 50.0. Moderate-sparsity results remain useful, but comparisons against weaker external models do not establish preservation of the original backbone’s accuracy.

The efficiency evidence does not adequately isolate the proposed sparsification. Table 1 reports a 2.72× speedup for 100-frame VGGT-S25, exceeding what removal of 25% of attention computation alone could explain under an otherwise identical implementation. Kernel and precision differences might explain this, but the paper lacks a matched dense-kernel control, runtime decomposition, and sufficient timing-protocol details. This matters because acceleration is the central contribution.

The methodological advance over existing sparse attention is limited and insufficiently isolated. Pooled query/key mask prediction and block-sparse execution closely follow the cited prior methods; the principal adaptations are the combined selection rule and special-token handling. Although the latter is ablated, there is no direct accuracy–runtime comparison against SpargeAttention or a controlled comparison of CDF-only, top-k-only, and combined selection. The claimed advantage of the proposed adaptive mechanism is therefore not established.

Sparsity reporting makes the operating points difficult to reproduce. Section 5 defines sparsity as the fraction of computed entries but then uses the skipped-entry speedup formula 1/(1−x). Table 1 does not explain how S25/S50/S75 map to thresholds or measured sparsity; for example, the 25-frame VGGT-S50 accuracy matches the supplementary configuration reporting 25.37% sparsity. Moreover, identical sparsity values recur across several datasets and sequence lengths despite input-adaptive selection, without explaining whether these are measured averages or reference values.

There are correctable technical specification errors and gaps. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask before softmax, which assigns positive probability to excluded entries rather than removing them; masked logits should be excluded or set to negative infinity. Section 4.2 also does not explain how dense special-token interactions and sparse patch interactions share the correct softmax normalization. These issues do not prove the implementation is wrong, but impede verification. Overall, the useful empirical gains are outweighed by unresolved attribution, reproducibility, and claim-support concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction with a training-free modification that works on both VGGT and π3, without changing their encoders or prediction heads.

Table 1 demonstrates useful operating points: on 200-frame inputs, VGGT-S25 reduces runtime from 18 to 8.5 seconds while RRA@5 changes from 83.9 to 83.1; π3-S25 reduces runtime from 13.9 to 6.8 seconds with a similarly small accuracy loss.

Evaluation covers nine datasets, two architectures, pose and geometry estimation, and multiple sequence lengths. The supplementary parameter sweeps provide substantial evidence about the accuracy–sparsity trade-off.

The special-token treatment is motivated and experimentally supported: Figure A-1 shows that preserving interactions involving camera and register tokens improves robustness, particularly for reconstruction at high sparsity. The learned-projection ablation also supports the simpler training-free design.
weaknesses: The headline claim of up to 4× acceleration with comparable performance conflates different operating points. At 100 frames, VGGT-S75 approaches this speedup (7.9 to 2.1 seconds), but RRA@5 falls from 84.8 to 58.1 and RTA@5 from 81.3 to 61.5. Moderate settings are useful, but the fastest settings do not preserve pose accuracy.

The central efficiency evidence lacks a controlled comparison separating sparsification from kernel and precision changes. The paper uses SpargeAttention infrastructure but does not report an otherwise identical dense-kernel baseline, a direct SpargeAttention comparison, or a runtime breakdown including mask construction. Consequently, the source of the substantial speed gains remains insufficiently established.

Sparsity reporting is inconsistent in ways that affect interpretation. Section 5 defines sparsity as the fraction of computed entries, while its speedup formula assumes the fraction omitted. Moreover, Table 1's 25-frame VGGT-S50 accuracy matches the supplementary configuration with 25.37% achieved sparsity, while VGGT-S25 matches one with 13.69%. The mapping between named variants, thresholds, measured sparsity, and timing needs to be explicit.

The methodological novelty is relatively narrow: pooled query–key mask prediction and block-sparse kernels build closely on existing attention methods. Preserving special-token interactions is useful, but the absence of a direct comparison with the cited sparsification method limits evidence for the proposed design's added value.

There are correctable technical specification problems. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask before softmax, which leaves omitted entries with nonzero probability; masked logits should instead be excluded or set to negative infinity. Section 4.2 also does not explain how patch and special-token attention share the required softmax normalization. These issues do not prove the implementation is incorrect, but impede faithful reproduction.

Overall, the demonstrated practical gains and broad evaluation place the paper near acceptance, but uncertainty about the efficiency comparison and the mismatch between the headline accuracy claim and the fastest results prevent a clear acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction with a training-free modification that transfers across VGGT, π3, and MapAnything. Its combination of pooled query–key block selection and dense interactions involving special tokens is simple and potentially useful.

Evaluation is unusually broad: three model families, multiple pose and pointmap benchmarks, Tanks & Temples sequences, and 50 ScanNet sequences with up to 1,000 frames. This provides substantial evidence that the approach generalizes beyond one architecture or dataset.

The moderate-sparsity operating points offer a convincing efficiency–accuracy trade-off. Figure A-1 reports approximately 2× acceleration on longer sequences around 60% sparsity; Table A-16 shows π3 retaining ATE 0.154 versus approximately 0.150 for the dense baseline. This practical contribution supports weak acceptance despite the reservations below.

The ablations substantiate important design choices. Figures 10 and A-2 demonstrate the benefit of preserving special-token interactions, while Figure A-3 shows that learned projections offer little improvement over the training-free method. Attention visualizations and layer-removal experiments provide additional useful empirical analysis.
weaknesses: The headline claim of matched accuracy with more than 3× acceleration is too broad. The strongest accuracy preservation occurs at lower speed-ups. At approximately 76% sparsity on 1,000-frame ScanNet, π3 ATE rises from approximately 0.150 to 0.180. Table A-3 also shows VGGT CO3D AUC@30 falling from 0.908 at low sparsity to 0.795 near 75% sparsity. Remaining competitive with other methods does not establish preservation of the original model’s accuracy.

Originality is primarily an adaptation of existing block-sparse attention: pooled query–key scoring, CDF selection, and the execution kernel build closely on prior work. The combined selection rule and special-token handling have value, but superiority over the strongest prior implementation is not fully established. Figure 10 disables SpargeAttention’s Hilbert permutation, and comparisons emphasize accuracy versus sparsity rather than accuracy versus measured latency.

Efficiency reporting is insufficiently reproducible for a central claim. Figure A-1 explicitly acknowledges inaccurate MapAnything timing, while the manuscript lacks a clear timing protocol covering synchronization, warm-up, repetitions, numerical precision, and preprocessing boundaries. It also does not separately quantify mask-construction overhead or peak memory. These omissions limit confidence in the exact acceleration and scalability claims.

The mathematical specification contains correctable errors and ambiguities. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero softmax probability; excluded logits should instead be masked with negative infinity. Section 5 defines effective sparsity as the computed fraction but subsequently uses it as the omitted fraction. Appendix Equation (6) omits the global-layer multiplicity. Section 4.2 should also specify how dense special-token interactions and sparse patch interactions share softmax normalization. These issues do not prove an implementation error, but prevent faithful implementation directly from the equations.

The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence. Maximum/mean attention statistics and selected correspondence visualizations do not quantify geometric matching accuracy or the true attention mass retained by pooled block selection. Layer removal demonstrates sensitivity to perturbation, but does not by itself establish exhaustive correspondence search. The supplementary MapAnything results also show a different layer-importance pattern, limiting the generality of the middle-layer explanation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in multi-view reconstruction with a training-free modification applicable to VGGT, π3, and MapAnything. Acceleration without retraining or changing prediction heads has clear utility.

Evaluation is substantial: three architectures, multiple pose and reconstruction benchmarks, extensive sparsity sweeps, and ScanNet sequences up to 1,000 frames. Figure A-1 supports useful operating points around 2× acceleration with relatively small pose degradation, particularly for π3.

The ablations support meaningful design choices. Figure 10 and Figure A-2 demonstrate the benefits of preserving dense special-token interactions and combining CDF selection with a minimum block budget. The learned-projection experiment also supports the simpler training-free approach.

Attention visualizations and layer-removal experiments provide useful empirical observations about these geometry transformers, while the supplementary tables expose trade-offs beyond the headline results.
weaknesses: The claim of matched accuracy with more than 3× acceleration is stronger than the evidence supports generally. Figure A-1 reaches the largest speedups at sparsities where accuracy deteriorates. Table A-16 shows π3 ATE increasing from 0.150 at low sparsity to 0.180 at approximately 76% sparsity. Reconstruction degradation can be considerably larger: in Table A-5, π3 accuracy/completeness errors increase from 0.107/0.085 at 8.65% sparsity to 0.386/0.222 at 77.03%. Remaining competitive with other models does not establish preservation of the original model's accuracy.

Originality is primarily a targeted adaptation of existing block-sparse attention: pooled query/key scoring, CDF selection, and the kernel come from established approaches. The adaptation has value, but comparative evidence is incomplete. Figure 10 disables SpargeAttention's Hilbert permutation and reports quality against sparsity rather than measured latency, leaving the practical advantage over the complete existing method uncertain.

Efficiency reporting lacks important reproducibility details. Figure A-1 acknowledges inaccurate MapAnything timing, and the manuscript does not adequately specify timing repetitions, synchronization, precision, or a breakdown of mask construction and sparse computation. Absolute latency and peak-memory measurements for the long-sequence experiments would make the scalability claims substantially more assessable.

The mathematical specification needs correction. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero softmax probability; exclusion requires negative-infinity masking or an explicitly restricted softmax. Section 5 defines sparsity as the computed fraction while its speedup formula treats it as the omitted fraction. Appendix Equation (6) also omits the global-layer multiplier. These appear correctable, but the text additionally leaves unclear how separately described patch/special attention computations preserve joint softmax normalization; the errors do not by themselves prove the implementation is incorrect.

Overall, the demonstrated training-free acceleration and broad evaluation place this near acceptance, but the overstated accuracy-preservation claim, incomplete comparison with the closest method, and insufficiently specified efficiency measurements keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper addresses a consequential bottleneck in feed-forward multi-view reconstruction with a practical, training-free modification. Compatibility with VGGT, π3, and MapAnything gives the contribution usefulness beyond a single architecture.

The evaluation is substantial: nine datasets, pose and pointmap estimation, three backbones, and ScanNet sequences extending to 1,000 frames. Figure A-1 supports useful operating points around 2× acceleration with relatively modest accuracy degradation, particularly for π3.

The design choices receive meaningful empirical support. Figure 10 and Figure A-2 demonstrate benefits from combining top-k and CDF selection and preserving dense interactions involving special tokens. The learned-projection ablation also supports the simpler training-free design.

Attention visualizations and layer-removal experiments provide informative analysis of existing geometry transformers. Together with the broad empirical validation, this practical contribution supports weak acceptance despite limited algorithmic novelty and reservations about the strongest claims.
weaknesses: The headline claim of more than 3× acceleration while matching original-model accuracy is stronger than the evidence supports generally. Figure A-1 reaches its largest speedups at sparsities where accuracy deteriorates. Table A-3 shows VGGT CO3Dv2 AUC@30 declining from 0.908 at 7.63% sparsity to 0.795 at 74.79%; Table A-5 shows π3 ETH3D reconstruction accuracy error increasing from 0.107 to 0.386 between low and high sparsity. Remaining competitive with other models does not establish preservation of the original model’s accuracy.

Novelty primarily lies in adapting established block-sparse attention to geometry transformers. The closest-baseline comparison is incomplete: Figure 10 disables SpargeAttention’s Hilbert permutation, and comparisons emphasize accuracy versus sparsity rather than measured latency at matched accuracy. Consequently, the advantage over a fully configured existing sparse-attention method is not firmly established.

Efficiency reporting lacks important reproducibility details. Figure A-1 explicitly acknowledges inaccurate MapAnything timing, while the manuscript does not adequately specify timing repetitions, synchronization, precision, or mask-construction overhead. Absolute latency and peak-memory measurements for the long-sequence configurations would make the scalability evidence substantially easier to assess.

There are correctable mathematical inconsistencies. Equation (2) multiplies logits by a binary mask, which leaves excluded entries with nonzero softmax probability; proper exclusion requires negative-infinity masking or an explicitly restricted softmax. Section 5 defines sparsity as the computed fraction but subsequently uses it as the skipped fraction. Appendix A also reverses the dense convention in its opening and omits the global-layer multiplicity in Equation (6). These errors weaken the formal exposition, although they do not establish that the implementation is incorrect.

The interpretation of attention as geometric correspondence search remains suggestive rather than demonstrated quantitatively. Qualitative matches and layer sensitivity do not measure correspondence correctness or retained attention mass, and Appendix C.3 finds a different layer-importance pattern for MapAnything. This limits the generality of the proposed mechanistic explanation.
